set.p: Scene: The Study and General Sitting-room, St Dominic's Vicarage, Victoria Park, London. Time: October 1894. ACT I Morning ACT II Afternoon ACT III Evening

div.head: ACT I
div.stage: A fine morning in October 1894 in the north east quarter of London, a vast district miles away from the London of Mayfair and St James's, and much less narrow, squalid, fetid and airless in its slums. It is strong in unfashionable middle class life: wide-streeted; myriad-populated; well served with ugly iron urinals, Radical clubs, and tram lines carrying a perpetual stream of yellow cars; enjoying in its main thoroughfares the luxury of grass-grown ‘front gardens’ untrodden by the foot of man save as to the path from the gate to the hall doors blighted by a callously endured monotony of miles and miles of unlovely brick houses, black iron railings, stony pavements, slated roofs, and respectably ill dressed or disreputably worse dressed people, quite accustomed to the place, and mostly plodding uninterestedly about somebody else's work. The little energy and eagerness that crop up shew themselves in cockney cupidity and business ‘push’. Even the policemen and the chapels are not infrequent enough to break the monotony. The sun is shining cheerfully: there is no fog; and though the smoke effectually prevents anything, whether faces and hands or bricks and mortar, from looking fresh and clean, it is not hanging heavily enough to trouble a Londoner. This desert of unattractiveness has its oasis. Near the outer end of the Hackney Road is a park of 217 acres, fenced in, not by railings, but by a wooden paling, and containing plenty of greensward, trees, a lake for bathers, flower beds which are triumphs of the admired cockney art of carpet gardening, and a sandpit, originally imported from the seaside for the delight of children, but speedily deserted on its becoming a natural vermin preserve for all the petty fauna of Kingsland, Hackney, and Hoxton. A bandstand, an unfurnished forum for religious, anti-religious, and political orators, cricket pitches, a gymnasium, and an old fashioned stone kiosk are among its attracttions. Wherever the prospect is bounded by trees or rising green grounds, it is a pleasant place. Where the ground stretches flat to the grey palings, with bricks and mortar, sky signs, crowded chimneys and smoke beyond, the prospect makes it desolate and sordid. The best view of Victoria Park is commanded by the front window of St Dominic's Parsonage, from which not a brick is visible. The parsonage is semi-detached, with a front garden and a porch. Visitors go up the flight of steps to the porch: tradespeople and members of the family go down by a door under the steps to the basement, with a breakfast room, used for all meals, in front, and the kitchen at the back. Upstairs, on the level of the hall door, is the drawingroom, with its large plate glass window looking out on the park. In this, the only sitting room that can be spared from the children and the family meals, the parson, the Reverend James Mavor Morell, does his work. He is sitting in a strong round backed revolving chair at the end of a long table, which stands across the window, so that he can cheer himself with a view of the park over his left shoulder. At the opposite end of the table, adjoining it, is a little table only half as wide as the other, with a typewriter on it. His typist is sitting at this machine, with her back to the window. The large table is littered with pamphlets, journals, letters, nests of drawers, an office diary, postage scales and the like. A spare chair for visitors having business with the parson is in the middle, turned to his end. Within reach of his hand is a stationery case, and a photograph in a frame. The wall behind him is fitted with bookshelves, on which an adept eye can measure the parson's casuistry and divinity by Maurice's Theological Essays and a complete set of Browning's poems, and the reformer's politics by a yellow backed Progress and Poverty, Fabian Essays, A Dream of John Ball, Marx's Capital, and half a dozen other literary landmarks in Socialism. Facing him on the other side of the room, near the typewriter, is the door. Further down opposite the fireplace, a bookcase stands on a cellaret, with a sofa near it. There is a generous fire burning; and the hearth, with a comfortable armchair and a black japanned flower-painted coal scuttle at one side, a miniature chair for children on the other, a varnished wooden mantelpiece, with neatly moulded shelves, tiny bits of mirror let into the panels, a travelling clock in a leather case (the inevitable wedding present), and on the wall above a large autotype of the chief figure in Titian's Assumption of the Virgin, is very inviting. Altogether the room is the room of a good housekeeper, vanquished, as far as the table is concerned, by an untidy man, but elsewhere mistress of the situation. The furniture, in its ornamental aspect, betrays the style of the advertized ‘drawingroom suite’ of the pushing suburban furniture dealer; but there is nothing useless or pretentious in the room, money being too scarce in the house of an east end parson to be wasted on snobbish trimmings. The Reverend James Mavor Morell is a Christian Socialist clergyman of the Church of England, and an active member of the Guild of St Matthew and the Christian Social Union. A vigorous, genial, popular man of forty, robust and goodlooking, full of energy, with pleasant, hearty, considerate manners, and a sound unaffected voice, which he uses with the clean athletic articulation of a practised orator, and with a wide range and perfect command of expression. He is a first rate clergyman, able to say what he likes to whom he likes, to lecture people without setting himself up against them, to impose his authority on them without humiliating them, and, on occasion, to interfere in their business without impertinence. His well-spring of enthusiasm and sympathetic emotion has never run dry for a moment: he still eats and sleeps heartily enough to win the daily battle between exhaustion and recuperation triumphantly. Withal, a great baby, pardonably vain of his powers and unconsciously pleased with himself. He has a healthy complexion: good forehead, with the brows somewhat blunt, and the eyes bright and eager, mouth resolute but not particularly well cut, and a substantial nose, with the mobile spreading nostrils of the dramatic orator, void, like all his features, of subtlety. The typist, Miss Proserpine Garnett, is a brisk little woman of about 30, of the lower middle class, neatly but cheaply dressed in a black merino skirt and a blouse, notably pert and quick of speech, and not very civil in her manner, but sensitive and affectionate. She is clattering away busily at her machine whilst Morell opens the last of his morning's letters. He realizes its contents with a comic groan of despair.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Another lecture?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Yes. The Hoxton Freedom Group want me to address them on Sunday morning
sp.stage: [he lays great emphasis on Sunday, this being the unreasonable part of the business].
sp.p: What are they?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Communist Anarchists, I think.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Just like Anarchists not to know that they cant have a parson on Sunday! Tell them to come to church if they want to hear me: it will do them good. Say I can come on Mondays and Thursdays only. Have you the diary there?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Have I any lecture on for next Monday?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Tower Hamlets Radical Club.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Well, Thursday then?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: English Land Restoration League.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: What next?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Guild of St Matthew on Monday. Independent Labor Party, Greenwich Branch, on Thursday. Monday, Social-Democratic Federation, Mile End Branch. Thursday, first Confirmation class.
Oh, I'd better tell them you cant come. Theyre only half a dozen ignorant and conceited costermongers without five shillings between them.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Ah; but you see theyre near relatives of mine.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Relatives of yours!

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Yes: we have the same father—in Heaven.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Oh, is that all?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [with a sadness which is a luxury to a man whose voice expresses it so finely]
sp.p: Ah, you dont believe it. Everybody says it: nobody believes it: nobody.
Well, well! Come, Miss Proserpine: cant you find a date for the costers? what about the 25th? That was vacant the day before yesterday.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Engaged. The Fabian Society.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Bother the Fabian Society! Is the 28th gone too?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: City dinner. Youre invited to dine with the Founders' Company.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Thatll do: I'll go to the Hoxton Group of Freedom instead.
sp.stage: [She enters the engagement in silence, with implacable disparagement of the Hoxton Anarchists in every line of her face. Morell bursts open the cover of a copy of The Church Reformer, which has come by post, and glances through Mr Stewart Headlam's leader and the Guild of St Matthew news. These proceedings are presently enlivened by the appearance of Morell's curate, the Reverend Alexander Mill, a young gentleman gathered by Morell from the nearest University settlement, whither he had come from Oxford to give the east end of London the benefit of his university training. He is a conceitedly well intentioned, enthusiastic, immature novice, with nothing positively unbearable about him except a habit of speaking with his lips carefully closed a full half inch from each corner for the sake of a finicking articulation and a set of university vowels, this being his chief means so far of bringing his Oxford refinement (as he calls his habits) to bear on Hackney vulgarity. Morell, whom he has won over by a doglike devotion, looks up indulgently from The Church Reformer, and remarks]
sp.p: Well, Lexy? Late again, as usual!

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: I'm afraid so. I wish I could get up in the morning.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Ha! ha!
Watch and pray. Lexy: watch and pray.

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: I know.
But how can I watch and pray when I am asleep? Isnt that so, Miss Prossy?
sp.stage: [He makes for the warmth of the fire].

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Miss Garnett, if you please.

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: I beg your pardon. Miss Garnett.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Youve got to do all the work today.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Never mind why. It will do you good to earn your supper before you eat it, for once in a way, as I do. Come! dont dawdle. You should have been off on your rounds half an hour ago.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Is she in earnest, Morell?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [in the highest spirits; his eyes dancing]
sp.p: Yes. I am going to dawdle today.

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: You! You dont know how.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Ha! ha! Dont I? I'm going to have this morning all to myself. My wife's coming back; she's due here at 11.45.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Coming back already! with the children? I thought they were to stay to the end of the month.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: So they are: she's only coming up for two days, to get some flannel things for Jimmy, and to see how we're getting on without her.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: But, my dear Morell, if what Jimmy and Fluffy had was scarlatina, do you think it wise—

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Scarlatina! Rubbish! it was German measles. I brought it into the house myself from the Pycroft Street school. A parson is like a doctor, my boy: he must face infection as a soldier must face bullets.
sp.stage: [He claps Lexy manfully on the shoulders].
sp.p: Catch the measles if you can, Lexy: she'll nurse you; and what a piece of luck that will be for you! Eh?

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: It's so hard to understand you about Mrs Morell—

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Ah, my boy, get married; get married to a good woman; and then youll understand. Thats a foretaste of what will be best in the Kingdom of Heaven we are trying to establish on earth. That will cure you of dawdling. An honest man feels that he must pay Heaven for every hour of happiness with a good spell of hard unselfish work to make others happy. We have no more right to consume happiness without producing it than to consume wealth without producing it. Get a wife like my Candida; and youll always be in arrear with your repayment.
sp.stage: [He pats Lexy affectionately and moves to leave the room].

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: Oh, wait a bit: I forgot.
sp.stage: [Morell halts and turns with the door knob in his hand].
sp.p: Your father-in-law is coming round to see you.

div.stage: Morell, surprised and not pleased, shuts the door again, with a complete change of manner.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Mr Burgess?

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: Yes. I passed him in the park, arguing with somebody. He asked me to let you know that he was coming.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: But he hasnt called here for three years. Are you sure, Lexy? Youre not joking, are you?

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: No sir, really.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Hm! Time for him to take another look at Candida before she grows out of his knowledge.
sp.stage: [He resigns himself to the inevitable, and goes out].

div.stage: Lexy looks after him with beaming worship. Miss Garnett, not being able to shake Lexy, relieves her feelings by worrying the typewriter.

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: What a good man! What a thorough loving soul he is!
sp.stage: [He takes Morell's place at the table, making himself very comfortable as he takes out a cigaret].

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [impatiently, pulling the letter she has been working at off the typewriter and folding it]
sp.p: Oh, a man ought to be able to be fond of his wife without making a fool of himself about her.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Oh, Miss Prossy!

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [snatching at the stationery case for an envelope, in which she encloses the letter as she speaks]
sp.p: Candida here, and Candida there, and Candida everywhere!
It's enough to drive anyone out of their senses
sp.stage: [thumping the envelope to make it stick]
sp.p: to hear a woman raved about in that absurd manner merely because she's got good hair and a tolerable figure.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: I think her extremely beautiful, Miss Garnett.
sp.stage: [He takes the photograph up; looks at it; and adds, with even greater impressiveness]
sp.p: extremely beautiful. How fine her eyes are!

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Her eyes are not a bit better than mine: now!
sp.stage: [He puts down the photograph and stares austerely at her].
sp.p: And you know very well you think me dowdy and second rate enough.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Heaven forbid that I should think of any of God's creatures in such a way!
sp.stage: [He moves stiffly away from her across the room to the neighborhood of the bookcase].

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Thank you. Thats very nice and comforting.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: I had no idea you had any feeling against Mrs Morell.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: I have no feeling against her. She's very nice, very good-hearted: I'm very fond of her, and can appreciate her real qualities far better than any man can.
sp.stage: [He shakes his head sadly. She rises and comes at him with intense pepperiness].
sp.p: You dont believe me? You think I'm jealous? Oh, what a knowledge of the human heart you have, Mr Lexy Mill! How well you know the weaknesses of Woman, dont you? It must be so nice to be a man and have a fine penetrating intellect instead of mere emotions like us, and to know that the reason we dont share your amorous delusions is that we're all jealous of one another!
sp.stage: [She abandons him with a toss of her shoulders, and crosses to the fire to warm her hands].

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: Ah, if you women only had the same clue to Man's strength that you have to his weakness, Miss Prossy, there would be no Woman Question.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [over her shoulder, as she stoops, holding her hands to the blaze]
sp.p: Where did you hear Morell say that? You didnt invent it yourself: youre not clever enough.

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: That's quite true, I am not ashamed of owing him that, as I owe him so many other spiritual truths. He said it at the annual conference of the Women's Liberal Federation. Allow me to add that though they didnt appreciate it, I, a mere man, did.
sp.stage: [He turns to the bookcase again, hoping that this may leave her crushed].

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [putting her hair straight at a panel of mirror in the mantelpiece]
sp.p: Well, when you talk to me, give me your own ideas, such as they are, and not his. You never cut a poorer figure than when you are trying to imitate him.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: I try to follow his example, not to imitate him.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [coming at him again on her way back to her work]
sp.p: Yes, you do: you imitate him. Why do you tuck your umbrella under your left arm instead of carrying it in your hand like anyone else? Why do you walk with your chin stuck out before you, hurrying along with that eager look in your eyes? you! who never get up before half past nine in the morning. Why do you say ‘knoaledge’ in church, though you always say ‘knolledge’ in private conversation! Bah! do you think I dont know?
Here! come and set about your work: weve wasted enough time for one morning. Here's a copy of the diary for today.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Thank you.
sp.stage: [He takes it and stands at the table with his back to her, reading it. She begins to transcribe her shorthand notes on the typewriter without troubling herself about his feelings].

div.stage: The door opens; and Mr Burgess enters unannounced. He is a man of sixty, made coarse and sordid by the compulsory selfishness of petty commerce, and later on softened into sluggish bumptiousness by overfeeding and commercial success. A vulgar ignorant guzzling man, offensive and contemptuous to people whose labor is cheap, respectful to wealth and rank, and quite sincere and without rancor or envy in both attitudes. The world has offered him no decently paid work except that of a sweater; and he has become, in consequence, somewhat hoggish. But he has no suspicion of this himself, and honestly regards his commercial prosperity as the inevitable and socially wholesome triumph of the ability, industry, shrewdness, and experience in business of a man who in private is easygoing, affectionate, and humorously convivial to a fault. Corporeally he is podgy, with a snoutish nose in the centre of a flat square face, a dust colored beard with a patch of grey in the centre under his chin, and small watery blue eyes with a plaintively sentimental expression, which he transfers easily to his voice by his habit of pompously intoning his sentences.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [stopping on the threshold, and looking round]
sp.p: They told me Mr Morell was here.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: I'll fetch him for you.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Youre not the same young lady as hused to typewrite for him?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [grumbling on his way to the hearth-rug]
sp.p: No: she was young-er.
sp.stage: [Miss Garnett stares at him; then goes out, slamming the door].
sp.p: Startin on your rounds, Mr Mill?

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Yes: I must be off presently.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Dont let me detain you, Mr Mill. What I come about is private between me and Mr Morell.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: I have no intention of intruding, I am sure, Mr Burgess. Good morning.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Oh, good morning to you.

div.stage: Morell returns as Lexy is making for the door.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Off to work?

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Take my silk handkerchief and wrap your throat up. Theres a cold wind. Away with you.

div.stage: Lexy, more than consoled for Burgess's rudeness, brightens up and goes out.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Spoilin your korates as usu'l, James. Good mornin. When I pay a man, an' 'is livin depens on me, I keep him in 'is place.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I always keep my curates in their places as my helpers and comrades. If you get as much work out of your clerks and warehousemen as I do out of my curates, you must be getting rich pretty fast. Will you take your old chair.

div.stage: He points with curt authority to the armchair beside the fireplace; then takes the spare chair from the table and sits down at an unfamiliar distance from his visitor.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Just the same as never, James!

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: When you last called—it was about three years ago, I think—you said the same thing a little more frankly. Your exact words then were ‘Just as big a fool as ever, James!’

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Well, praps I did; but

I meant no hoffence by it. A clorgyman is privileged to be a bit of a fool, you know: it's ony becomin in 'is profession that he should. Anyhow, I come here, not to rake up hold differences, but to let bygones be bygones.
sp.stage: [Suddenly becoming very solemn, and approaching Morell]
sp.p: James: three years ago, you done me a hil turn. You done me hout of a contrac: as when I gev you arsh words in my natral disappointment, you turned my daughrter again me. Well, Ive come to hact the part of a Kerischin.
I forgive you, James.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Confound your impudence!

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [retreating, with almost lachrymose deprecation of this treatment]
sp.p: Is that becomin language for a clorgyman, James? And you so particlar, too!

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: No, sir: it is not becoming language for a clergyman. I used the wrong word. I should have said damn your impudence: thats what St Paul or any honest priest would have said to you. Do you think I have forgotten that tender of yours for the contract to supply clothing to the workhouse?

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: I hacted in the hinterest of the ratepayers, James. It was the lowest tender: you carnt deny that.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Yes, the lowest, because you paid worse wages than any other employer—starvation wages—aye, worse than starvation wages—to the women who made the clothing. Your wages would have driven them to the streets to keep body and soul together.
Those women were my parishioners. I shamed the Guardians out of accepting your tender: I shamed the ratepayers out of letting them do it: I shamed everybody but you.
How dare you, sir, come here and offer to forgive me, and talk about your daughter, and—

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Heasy, James! heasy! heasy! Dont git hinto a fluster about nothink. Ive howned I was wrong.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Have you? I didn't hear you.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Of course I did. I hown it now. Come: I harsk your pardon for the letter I wrote you. Is that enough?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Thats nothing. Have you raised the wages?

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: What!

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Ive turned a moddle hemployer. I dont hemploy no women now: theyre all sacked; and the work is done by machinery. Not a man 'as less than sixpence a hour; and the skilled ands gits the Trade Union rate.
What ave you to say to me now?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Is it possible! Well, theres more joy in heaven over one sinner that repenteth!—
sp.stage: [Going to Burgess with an explosion of apologetic cordiality]
sp.p: My dear Burgess: how splendid of you! I most heartily beg your pardon for my hard thoughts.
And now, dont you feel the better for the change? Come! confess! youre happier. You look happier.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Well, praps I do. I spose I must, since you notice it. At all events, I git my contrax assepted by the County Council.
They dussent ave nothink to do with me unless I paid fair wages: curse em for a parcel o meddlin fools!

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: So that was why you raised the wages!

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Woy helse should I do it? What does it lead to but drink and huppishness in workin men?
sp.stage: [He seats himself magisterially in the easy chair].
sp.p: It's hall very well for you, James: it gits you hinto the papers and makes a great man of you; but you never think of the arm you do, puttin money into the pockets of workin men that they dunno ow to spend, and takin it from people that might be makin a good huse on it.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [with a heavy sigh, speaking with cold politeness]
sp.p: What is your business with me this morning? I shall not pretend to believe that you are here merely out of family sentiment.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Yes I ham: just family sentiment and nothink helse.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I dont believe you.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Dont say that to me again, James Mavor Morell.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I'll say it just as often as may be necessary to convince you that it's true. I dont believe you.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [collapsing into an abyss of wounded feeling]
sp.p: Oh, well, if youre detormined to be hunfriendly, I spose I'd better go.
sp.stage: [He moves reluctantly towards the door. Morell makes no sign. He lingers].
sp.p: I didnt hexpect to find a hunforgivin spirit in you, James.
sp.stage: [Morell still not responding, he takes a few more reluctant steps doorwards. Then he comes back, whining].
sp.p: We huseter git on well enough, spite of our different hopinions. Woy are you so changed to me? I give you my word I come here in peeorr
frenliness, not wishin to be hon bad terms with my hown daughrter's usban. Come, James: be a Kerischin, and shake ands.
sp.stage: [He puts his hand sentimentally on Morell's shoulder].

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Look here, Burgess. Do you want to be as welcome here as you were before you lost that contract?

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: I do, James. I do—honest.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Then why dont you behave as you did then?

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Ow d'y'mean?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: I'll tell you. You thought me a young fool then.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: No I didnt, James. I—

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Yes, you did. And I thought you an old scoundrel.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [most vehemently deprecating this gross self-accusation on Morell's part]
sp.p: No you didnt, James. Now you do yourself a hinjustice.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Yes I did. Well, that did not prevent our getting on very well together. God made you what I call a scoundrel as He made me what you call a fool.
sp.stage: [The effect of this observation on Burgess is to remove the keystone of his moral arch. He becomes bodily weak, and, with his eyes fixed on Morell in a helpless stare, puts out his hand apprehensively to balance himself, as if the floor had suddenly sloped under him. Morell proceeds, in the same tone of quiet conviction]
sp.p: It was not for me to quarrel with His handiwork in the one case more than in the other. So long as you come here honestly as a self-respecting, thorough, convinced, scoundrel, justifying your scoundrelism and proud of it, you are welcome. But
sp.stage: [and now Morell's tone becomes formidable; and he rises and strikes the back of the chair for greater emphasis]
sp.p: I wont have you here snivelling about being a model employer and a converted man when youre only an apostate with your coat turned for the sake of a County Council contract.
sp.stage: [He nods at him to enforce the point; then goes to the hearth-rug, where he takes up a comfortably commanding position with his back to the fire, and continues]
sp.p: No: I like a man to be true to himself, even in wickedness. Come now: either take your hat and go; or else sit down and give me a good scoundrelly reason for wanting to be friends with me.
sp.stage: [Burgess, whose emotions have subsided sufficiently to be expressed by a dazed grin, is relieved by this concrete proposition. He ponders it for a moment, and then, slowly and very modestly sits down in the chair Morell has just left].
sp.p: Thats right. Now out with it.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Well, you orr a queer bird, James, and no mistake. But
one carnt elp likin you: besides, as I said afore, of course one dont take hall a clorgyman says seriously, or the world couldnt go on. Could it now?
sp.stage: [He composes himself for graver discourse, and, turning his eyes on Morell, proceeds with dull seriousness]
sp.p: Well, I dont mind tellin you, since it's your wish we should be free with one another, that I did think you a bit of a fool once; but I'm beginnin to think that praps I was be'ind the times a bit.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Aha! Youre finding that out at last, are you?

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Yes: times 'as changed mor'n I could a believed. Five yorr

ago, no sensible man would a thought o takin hup with your hidears. I hused to wonder you was let preach at all. Why, I know a clorgyman what 'as bin kep hout of his job for yorrs by the Bishop o London, although the pore feller's not a bit more religious than you are. But today, if hennyone was to horffer to bet me a thousan poun that youll hend by being a bishop yourself, I dussent take the bet.

You and your crew are gittin hinfluential: I can see that. Theyll ave to give you somethink someday, if it's honly to stop your mouth. You ad the right instinc arter all, James: the line you took is the payin line in the long run for a man o your sort.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Shake hands, Burgess. Now youre talking honestly. I dont think theyll make me a bishop; but if they do, I'll introduce you to the biggest jobbers I can get to come to my dinner parties.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [who has risen with a sheepish grin and accepted the hand of friendship]
sp.p: You will ave your joke, James. Our quarrel's made up now, ain it?

sp.speaker: A WOMAN'S VOICE.
sp.p: Say yes, James.

div.stage: Startled, they turn quickly and find that Candida has just come in, and is looking at them with an amused maternal indulgence which is her characteristic expression. She is a woman of 33, well built, well nourished, likely, one guesses, to become matronly later on, but now quite at her best, with the double charm of youth and motherhood. Her ways are those of a woman who has found that she can always manage people by engaging their affection, and who does so frankly and instinctively without the smallest scruple. So far, she is like any other pretty woman who is just clever enough to make the most of her sexual attractions for trivially selfish ends; but Candida's serene brow, courageous eyes, and well set mouth and chin signify largeness of mind and dignity of character to ennoble her cunning in the affections. A wise-hearted observer, looking at her, would at once guess that whoever had placed the Virgin of the Assumption over her hearth did so because he fancied some spiritual resemblance between them, and yet would not suspect either her husband or herself of any such idea, or indeed of any concern with the art of Titian. Just now she is in bonnet and mantle, carrying a strapped rug with her umbrella stuck through it, a handbag, and a supply of illustrated papers.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Candida! Why—
sp.stage: [he looks at his watch, and is horrified to find it so late].
sp.p: My darling!
sp.stage: [Hurrying to her and seizing the rug strap, pouring forth his remorseful regrets all the time]
sp.p: I intended to meet you at the train. I let the time slip.
I was so engrossed by—
—I forgot—oh!

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [a little shamefaced and doubtful of his reception]
sp.p: How orr you, Candy?
sp.stage: [She, still in Morell's arms, offers him her cheek, which he kisses].
sp.p: James and me is come to a nunner-stannin. A honorable unnerstannin. Ain we, James?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Oh bother your understanding! youve kept me late for Candida.
My poor love: how did you manage about the luggage? How—

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: There! there! there! I wasnt alone. Eugene has been down with us; and we travelled together.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Eugene!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Yes: he's struggling with my luggage, poor boy. Go out, dear, at once; or he'll pay for the cab; and I dont want that.
sp.stage: [Morell hurries out. Candida puts down her handbag; then takes off her mantle and bonnet and puts them on the sofa with the rug, chatting meanwhile].
sp.p: Well, papa: how are you getting on at home?

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: The ouse aint worth livin in since you left it, Candy. I wish youd come round and give the gurl a talkin to. Who's this Eugene thats come with you?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Oh, Eugene's one of James's discoveries. He found him sleeping on the Embankment last June. Havnt you noticed our new picture [pointing to the Virgin]? He gave us that.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Garn! D'you mean to tell me—your hown father!—that cab touts or such like, orf the Embankment, buys pictures like that?
Dont deceive me, Candy: it's a 'Igh Church picture; and James chose it hisself.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Guess again. Eugene isnt a cab tout.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Then what is he?
A nobleman, I spose.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Yes. His uncle's a peer! A real live earl.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [not daring to believe such good news]
sp.p: No!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Yes. He had a seven day bill for £55 in his pocket when James found him on the Embankment. He thought he couldnt get any money for it until the seven days were up; and he was too shy to ask for credit. Oh, he's a dear boy! We are very fond of him.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [pretending to belittle the aristocracy, but with his eyes gleaming]
sp.p: Hm! I thort you wouldnt git a hearl's nevvy visitin in Victawriar Pawrk unless he were a bit of a flat.
Of course I dont old with that picture, Candy; but still it's a 'igh class fust rate work of ort: I can see that. Be sure you hintrodooce me to im, Candy.
I can ony stay about two minutes.

div.stage: Morell comes back with Eugene, whom Burgess contemplates moist-eyed with enthusiasm. He is a strange, shy youth of eighteen, slight, effeminate, with a delicate childish voice, and a hunted tormented expression and shrinking manner that shew the painful sensitiveness of very swift and acute apprehensiveness in youth, before the character has grown to its full strength. Miserably irresolute, he does not know where to stand or what to do. He is afraid of Burgess, and would run away into solitude if he dared; but the very intensity with which he feels a perfectly commonplace position comes from excessive nervous force; and his nostrils, mouth, and eyes betray a fiercely petulant wilfulness, as to the bent of which his brow, already lined with pity, is reassuring. He is so uncommon as to be almost unearthly; and to prosaic people there is something noxious in this unearthliness, just as to poetic people there is something angelic in it. His dress is anarchic. He wears an old blue serge jacket, unbuttoned, over a woollen lawn tennis shirt, with a silk handkerchief for a cravat, trousers matching the jacket, and brown canvas shoes. In these garments he has apparently lain in the heather and waded through the waters; and there is no evidence of his having ever brushed them. As he catches sight of a stranger on entering, he stops, and edges along the wall on the opposite side of the room.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Come along: you can spare us quarter of an hour at all events. This is my father-in-law. Mr Burgess—Mr Marchbanks.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Glad to meet you, sir.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [crossing to him with great heartiness, whilst Morell joins Candida at the fire]
sp.p: Glad to meet you, I'm shore, Mr Morchbanks.
Ow do you find yoreself this weather? Ope you aint lettin James put no foolish ideas into your ed?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Foolish ideas? Oh, you mean Socialism? No.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Thats right.
Well, I must go now: theres no elp for it. Yore not comin my way, orr you, Mr Morchbanks?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Which way is that?

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Victawriar Pawrk Station. Theres a city train at 12.25.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Nonsense. Eugene will stay to lunch with us, I expect.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No—I—I—

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Well, well, I shornt press you: I bet youd rather lunch with Candy. Some night, I ope, youll come and dine with me at my club, the Freeman Founders in Nortn Folgit. Come: say you will!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Thank you, Mr Burgess. Where is Norton Folgate. Down in Surrey, isnt it?

div.stage: Burgess, inexpressibly tickled, begins to splutter with laughter.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Youll lose your train, papa, if you dont go at once. Come back in the afternoon and tell Mr Marchbanks where to find the club.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Down in Surrey! Har, har! thats not a bad one. Well, I never met a man as didnt know Nortn Folgit afore.
Goodbye, Mr Morchbanks: I know yore too ighbred to take my pleasantry in bad part.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Not at all.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Bye, bye, Candy. I'll look in again later on. So long, James.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Must you go?

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Dont stir.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Oh, I'll see you off.

div.stage: Eugene stares after them apprehensively, holding his breath until Burgess disappears.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Well, Eugene?
sp.stage: [He turns with a start, and comes eagerly towards her, but stops irresolutely as he meets her amused look].
sp.p: What do you think of my father?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I—I hardly know him yet. He seems to be a very nice old gentleman.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: And youll go to the Freeman Founders to dine with him, wont you?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Yes, if it will please you.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Do you know, you are a very nice boy, Eugene, with all your queerness. If you had laughed at my father I shouldnt have minded; but I like you ever so much better for being nice to him.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Ought I to have laughed? I noticed that he said something funny; but I am so ill at ease with strangers; and I never can see a joke. I'm very sorry.
sp.stage: [He sits down on the sofa, his elbows on his knees and his temples between his fists with an expression of hopeless suffering].

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Oh come! You great baby, you! You are worse than usual this morning. Why were you so melancholy as we came along in the cab?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Oh, that was nothing. I was wondering how much I ought to give the cabman. I know it's utterly silly; but you dont know how dreadful such things are to me—how I shrink from having to deal with strange people.
But it's all right. He beamed all over and touched his hat when Morell gave him two shillings. I was on the point of offering him ten.

div.stage: Morell comes back with a few letters and newspapers which have come by the midday post.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Oh, James dear, he was going to give the cabman ten shillings! ten shillings for a three minutes drive! Oh dear!

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [at the table, glancing through the letters]
sp.p: Never mind her, Marchbanks. The overpaying instinct is a generous one: better than the underpaying instinct, and not so common.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No: cowardice, incompetence. Mrs Morell's quite right.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Of course she is.
And now I must leave you to James for the present. I suppose you are too much of a poet to know the state a woman finds her house in when she's been away for three weeks. Give me my rug.
sp.stage: [Eugene takes the strapped rug from the couch, and gives it to her. She takes it in her left hand, having the bag in her right].
sp.p: Now hang my cloak across my arm.
Now my hat.
sp.stage: [He puts it into the hand which has the bag].
sp.p: Now open the door for me.
sp.stage: [He hurries before her and opens the door].
sp.p: Thanks.
sp.stage: [She goes out; and Marchbanks shuts the door].

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Youll stay to lunch, Marchbanks, of course.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: I mustnt.
sp.stage: [He glances quickly at Morell, but at once avoids his frank look, and adds, with obvious disingenuousness]
sp.p: I mean I cant.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: You mean you wont.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No: I should like to, indeed. Thank you very much. But—but—

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: But—but—but—but—Bosh! If youd like to stay, stay. If youre shy, go and take a turn in the park and write poetry until half past one; and then come in and have a good feed.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Thank you, I should like that very much. But I really musnt. The truth is, Mrs Morell told me not to. She said she didnt think youd ask me to stay to lunch, but that I was to remember, if you did, that you didnt really want me to.
She said I'd understand; but I dont. Please dont tell her I told you.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Oh, is that all? Wont my suggestion that you should take a turn in the park meet the difficulty?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Why, you duffer—
sp.stage: [But this boisterousness jars himself as well as Eugene. He checks himself].
sp.p: No: I wont put it in that way.
sp.stage: [He comes to Eugene with affectionate seriousness].
sp.p: My dear lad: in a happy marriage like ours, there is something very sacred in the return of the wife to her home.
sp.stage: [Marchbanks looks quickly at him, half anticipating his meaning].
sp.p: An old friend or a truly noble and sympathetic soul is not in the way on such occasions; but a chance visitor is.
sp.stage: [The hunted horrorstricken expression comes out with sudden vividness in Eugene's face as he understands. Morell, occupied with his own thoughts, goes on without noticing this].
sp.p: Candida thought I would rather not have you here; but she was wrong. I'm very fond of you, my boy; and I should like you to see for yourself what a happy thing it is to be married as I am.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Happy! Your marriage! You think that! You believe that!

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I know it, my lad. Larochefoucauld said that there are convenient marriages but no delightful ones. You dont know the comfort of seeing through and through a thundering liar and rotten cynic like that fellow. Ha! ha! Now, off with you to the park, and write your poem. Half past one, sharp, mind: we never wait for anybody.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No: stop: you shant. I'll force it into the light.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Eh? Force what?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I must speak to you. There is something that must be settled between us.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [with a whimsical glance at his watch]
sp.p: Now?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Now. Before you leave this room.
sp.stage: [He retreats a few steps, and stands as if to bar Morell's way to the door].

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [without moving, and gravely, perceiving now that there is something serious the matter]
sp.p: I'm not going to leave it, my dear boy: I thought you were.
sp.stage: [Eugene, baffled by his firm tone, turns his back on him, writhing with anger. Morell goes to him and puts his hand on his shoulder strongly and kindly, disregarding his attempt to shake it off].
sp.p: Come: sit down quietly; and tell me what it is: And remember: we are friends, and need not fear that either of us will be anything but patient and kind to the other, whatever we may have to say.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Oh, I am not forgetting myself: I am only
sp.stage: [covering his face desperately with his hands]
sp.p: full of horror.
sp.stage: [Then, dropping his hands, and thrusting his face forward fiercely at Morell, he goes on threateningly]
sp.p: You shall see whether this is a time for patience and kindness.
sp.stage: [Morell, firm as a rock, looks indulgently at him].
sp.p: Dont look at me in that self-complacent way. You think yourself stronger than I am; but I shall stagger you if you have a heart in your breast.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Stagger me, my boy. Out with it.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: First—

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: First?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I love your wife.

div.stage: Morell recoils, and, after staring at him for a moment in utter amazement, bursts into uncontrollable laughter. Eugene is taken aback; but not disconcerted; and he soon becomes indignant and contemptuous.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [sitting down to have his laugh out]
sp.p: Why, my dear child, of course you do. Everybody loves her: they cant help it. I like it. But
I say, Eugene: do you think yours is a case to be talked about? Youre under twenty: she's over thirty. Doesnt it look rather too like a case of calf love?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: You dare say that of her! You think that way of the love she inspires! It is an insult to her!

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: To her! Eugene: take care. I have been patient. I hope to remain patient. But there are some things I wont allow. Dont force me to shew you the indulgence I should shew to a child. Be a man.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [with a gesture as if sweeping something behind him]
sp.p: Oh, let us put aside all that cant. It horrifies me when I think of the doses of it she has had to endure in all the weary years during which you have selfishly and blindly sacrificed her to minister to your self-sufficiency: you!
who have not one thought—one sense—in common with her.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: She seems to bear it pretty well.
Eugene, my boy: you are making a fool of yourself: a very great fool of yourself. Theres a piece of wholesome plain speaking for you.
sp.stage: [He knocks in the lesson with a nod in his old way, and posts himself on the hearth-rug, holding his hands behind him to warm them].

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Oh, do you think I dont know all that? Do you think that the things people make fools of themselves about are any less real and true than the things they behave sensibly about?
sp.stage: [Morell's gaze wavers for the first time. He forgets to warm his hands, and stands listening, startled and thoughtful].
sp.p: They are more true: they are the only things that are true. You are very calm and sensible and moderate with me because you can see that I am a fool about your wife; just as no doubt that old man who was here just now is very wise over your Socialism, because he sees that you are a fool about it.
sp.stage: [Morell's perplexity deepens markedly. Eugene follows up his advantage, plying him fiercely with questions].
sp.p: Does that prove you wrong? Does your complacent superiority to me prove that I am wrong?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Marchbanks: some devil is putting these words into your mouth. It is easy—terribly easy—to shake a man's faith in himself. To take advantage of that to break a man's spirit is devil's work. Take care of what you are doing. Take care.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: I know. I'm doing it on purpose. I told you I should stagger you.

div.stage: They confront one another threateningly for a moment. Then Morell recovers his dignity.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Eugene: listen to me. Some day, I hope and trust, you will be a happy man like me.
sp.stage: [Eugene chafes intolerantly, repudiating the worth of his happiness. Morell, deeply insulted, controls himself with fine forbearance, and continues steadily with great artistic beauty of delivery]
sp.p: You will be married; and you will be working with all your might and valor to make every spot on earth as happy as your own home. You will be one of the makers of the Kingdom of Heaven on earth; and—who knows?----you may be a master builder where I am only a humble journeyman; for dont think, my boy, that I cannot see in you, young as you are, promise of higher powers than I can ever pretend to. I well know that it is in the poet that the holy spirit of man—the god within him—is most godlike. It should make you tremble to think of that—to think that the heavy burthen and great gift of a poet may be laid upon you.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [unimpressed and remorseless, his boyish crudity of assertion telling sharply against Morell's oratory]
sp.p: It does not make me tremble. It is the want of it in others that makes me tremble.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [redoubling his force of style under the stimulus of his genuine feeling and Eugene's obduracy]
sp.p: Then help to kindle it in them—in me—not to extinguish it. In the future, when you are as happy as I am, I will be your true brother in the faith. I will help you to believe that God has given us a world that nothing but our own folly keeps from being a paradise. I will help you to believe that every stroke of your work is sowing happiness for the great harvest that all—even the humblest—shall one day reap. And last, but trust me, not least, I will help you to believe that your wife loves you and is happy in her home. We need such help, Marchbanks: we need it greatly and always. There are so many things to make us doubt, if once we let our understanding be troubled. Even at home, we sit as if in camp, encompassed by a hostile army of doubts. Will you play the traitor and let them in on me?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Is it like this for her here always? A woman, with a great soul, craving for reality, truth, freedom; and being fed on metaphors, sermons, stale perorations, mere rhetoric. Do you think a woman's soul can live on your talent for preaching?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Marchbanks: you make it hard for me to control myself. My talent is like yours insofar as it has any real worth at all. It is the gift of finding words for divine truth.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: It's the gift of the gab, nothing more and nothing less. What has your knack of fine talking to do with the truth, any more than playing the organ has? Ive never been in your church; but Ive been to your political meetings; and Ive seen you do whats called rousing the meeting to enthusiasm: that is, you excited them until they behaved exactly as if they were drunk. And their wives looked on and saw what fools they were. Oh, it's an old story: youll find it in the Bible. I imagine King David, in his fits of enthusiasm, was very like you.
‘But his wife despised him in her heart.’

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Leave my house. Do you hear?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Let me alone. Dont touch me.
sp.stage: [Morell grasps him powerfully by the lappell of his coat: he cowers down on the sofa and screams passionately]
sp.p: Stop, Morell: if you strike me, I'll kill myself: I wont bear it.
Let me go. Take your hand away.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: You little snivelling, cowardly whelp.
Go, before you frighten yourself into a fit.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [on the sofa, gasping, but relieved by the withdrawal of Morell's hand]
sp.p: I'm not afraid of you: it's you who are afraid of me.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: It looks like it, doesnt it?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Yes, it does.
sp.stage: [Morell turns away contemptuously. Eugene scrambles to his feet and follows him].
sp.p: You think because I shrink from being brutally handled—because

I can do nothing but cry with rage when I am met with violence—because I cant lift a heavy trunk down from the top of a cab like you—because I can't fight you for your wife as a drunken navvy would: all that makes you think I'm afraid of you. But youre wrong. If I havnt got what you call British pluck, I havnt British cowardice either: I'm not afraid of a clergyman's ideas. I'll fight your ideas. I'll rescue her from her slavery to them. I'll pit my own ideas against them. You are driving me out of the house because you darent let her choose between your ideas and mine. You are afraid to let me see her again.
sp.stage: [Morell, angered, turns suddenly on him. He flies to the door in involuntary dread].
sp.p: Let me alone, I say. I'm going.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Wait a moment: I am not going to touch you: dont be afraid. When my wife comes back she will want to know why you have gone. And when she finds that you are never going to cross our threshold again, she will want to have that explained too. Now I dont wish to distress her by telling her that you have behaved like a blackguard.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: You shall. You must. If you give any explanation but the true one, you are a liar and a coward. Tell her what I said; and how you were strong and manly, and shook me as a terrier shakes a rat; and how I shrank and was terrified; and how you called me a snivelling little whelp and put me out of the house. If you dont tell her, I will: I'll write it to her.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Why do you want her to know this?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Because she will understand me, and know that I understand her. If you keep back one word of it from her—if you are not ready to lay the truth at her feet as I am—then you will know to the end of your days that she really belongs to me and not to you. Goodbye.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Stop: I will not tell her.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Either the truth or a lie you must tell her, if I go.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Marchbanks: it is sometimes justifiable—

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: I know: to lie. It will be useless. Goodbye, Mr Clergyman.

div.stage: As he turns to the door, it opens and Candida enters in her housekeeping dress.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Are you going, Eugene?
Well, dear me, just look at you, going out into the street in that state.! You are a poet, certainly. Look at him, James!
sp.stage: [She takes him by the coat, and brings him forward, shewing him to Morell].
sp.p: Look at his collar! look at his tie! look at his hair! One would think somebody had been throttling you.
sp.stage: [Eugene instinctively tries to look round at Morell; but she pulls him back].
sp.p: Here! Stand still.
sp.stage: [She buttons his collar; ties his neckerchief in a bow; and arranges his hair].
sp.p: There! Now you look so nice that I think youd better stay to lunch after all, though I told you you mustnt. It will be ready in half an hour.
sp.stage: [She puts a final touch to the bow. He kisses her hand].
sp.p: Dont be silly.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I want to stay, of course; unless the reverend gentleman your husband has anything to advance to the contrary.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Shall he stay, James, if he promises to be a good boy and help me to lay the table?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Oh yes, certainly: he had better.
sp.stage: [He goes to the table and pretends to busy himself with his papers there].

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Come and lay the table.
sp.stage: [She takes it. They go to the door together. As they pass out he adds]
sp.p: I am the happiest of mortals.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: So was I—an hour ago.

div.head: ACT II
div.stage: The same day later in the afternoon. The same room. The chair for visitors has been replaced at the table. Marchbanks, alone and idle, is trying to find out how the typewriter works. Hearing someone at the door, he steals guiltily away to the window and pretends to be absorbed in the view. Miss Garnett, carrying the notebook in which she takes down Morell's letters in shorthand from his dictation, sits down at the typewriter and sets to work transcribing them, much too busy to notice Eugene. When she begins the second line she stops and stares at the machine. Something wrong evidently.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Bother! Youve been meddling with my typewriter, Mr Marchbanks; and theres not the least use in your trying to look as if you hadnt.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: I'm very sorry, Miss Garnett. I only tried to make it write.
But it wouldnt.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Well, youve altered the spacing.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: I assure you I didn't. I didnt indeed. I only turned a little wheel. It gave a sort of click.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Oh, now I understand.
sp.stage: [She restores the spacing, talking volubly all the time].
sp.p: I suppose you thought it was a sort of barrel-organ. Nothing to do but turn the handle, and it would write a beautiful love letter for you straight off, eh?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: I suppose a machine could be made to write love letters. Theyre all the same, arnt they?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [somewhat indignantly: any such discussion, except by way of pleasantry, being outside her code of manners]
sp.p: How do I know? Why do you ask me?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I beg your pardon. I thought clever people—people who can do business and write letters and that sort of thing—always had to have love affairs to keep them from going mad.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Mr Marchbanks!
sp.stage: [She looks severely at him, and marches majestically to the bookcase].

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: I hope I havnt offended you. Perhaps I shouldnt have alluded to your love affairs.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [plucking a blue book from the shelf and turning sharply on him]
sp.p: I havnt any love affairs. How dare you say such a thing? The idea!
sp.stage: [She tucks the book under her arm, and is bouncing back to her machine when he addresses her with awakened interest and sympathy].

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Really! Oh, then you are shy, like me.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Certainly I am not shy. What do you mean?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: You must be: that is the reason there are so few love affairs in the world. We all go about longing for love: it is the first need of our natures, the first prayer of our hearts; but we dare not utter our longing: we are too shy.
Oh, Miss Garnett, what would you not give to be without fear, without shame—

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Well, upon my word!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Ah, dont say those stupid things to me: they dont deceive me: what use are they? Why are you afraid to be your real self with me? I am just like you.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Like me! Pray are you flattering me or flattering yourself I dont feel quite sure which.
sp.stage: [She again tries to get back to her work].

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Hush! I go about in search of love; and I find it in unmeasured stores in the bosoms of others. But when I try to ask for it, this horrible shyness strangles me, and I stand dumb, or worse than dumb, saying meaningless things foolish lies. And I see the affection I am longing for given to dogs and cats and pet birds, because they come and ask for it.
It must be asked for: it is like a ghost: it cannot speak unless it is first spoken to.
sp.stage: [At his usual pitch, but with deep melancholy]
sp.p: All the love in the world is longing to speak; only it dare not, because it is shy! shy! shy! That is the world's tragedy.
sp.stage: [With a deep sigh he sits in the visitors' chair and buries his face in his hands].

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [amazed, but keeping her wits about her: her point of honor in encounters with strange young men]
sp.p: Wicked people get over that shyness occasionally, dont they?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Wicked people means people who have no love: therefore they have no shame. They have the power to ask love because they dont need it: they have the power to offer it because they have none to give.
sp.stage: [He collapses into his seat, and adds, mournfully]
sp.p: But we, who have love, and long to mingle it with the love of others: we cannot utter a word.
You find that, dont you?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Look here: if you dont stop talking like this, I'll leave the room, Mr Marchbanks: I really will. It's not proper.

div.stage: She resumes her seat at the typewriter, opening the blue book and preparing to copy a passage from it.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Nothing thats worth saying is proper.
sp.stage: [He rises, and wanders about the room in his lost way].
sp.p: I cant understand you, Miss Garnett. What am I to talk about?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Talk about indifferent things. Talk about the weather.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Would you talk about indifferent things if a child were by, crying bitterly with hunger?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: I suppose not.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Well: I cant talk about indifferent things with my heart crying out bitterly in its hunger.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Then hold your tongue.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Yes: that is what it always comes to. We hold our tongues. Does that stop the cry of your heart? for it does cry: doesnt it? It must, if you have a heart.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [suddenly rising with her hand pressed on her heart]
sp.p: Oh, it's no use trying to work while you talk like that.
sp.stage: [She leaves her little table and sits on the sofa. Her feelings are keenly stirred].
sp.p: It's no business of yours whether my heart cries or not; but I have a mind to tell you, for all that.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: You neednt. I know already that it must.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: But mind! if you ever say I said so, I'll deny it.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Yes, I know. And so you havnt the courage to tell him?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Him! Who?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Whoever he is. The man you love. It might be anybody. The curate, Mr Mill, perhaps.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Mr Mill!!! A fine man to break my heart about, indeed! I'd rather have you than Mr Mill.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No, really: I'm very sorry; but you mustnt think of that. I—

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [testily, going to the fireplace and standing at it with her back to him]
sp.p: Oh, dont be frightened: it's not you. It's not any one particular person.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I know. You feel that you could love anybody that offered—

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Anybody that offered! No, I do not. What do you take me for?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No use. You wont make me real answers: only those things that everybody says.
sp.stage: [He strays to the sofa and sits down disconsolately].

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [nettled at what she takes to be a disparagement of her manners by an aristocrat]
sp.p: Oh well, if you want original conversation, youd better go and talk to yourself.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: That is what all poets do: they talk to themselves out loud; and the world overhears them. But it's horribly lonely not to hear someone else talk sometimes.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Wait until Mr Morell comes. He'll talk to you.
Oh, you neednt make wry faces over him: he can talk better than you.
He'd talk your little head off.
sp.stage: [She is going back angrily to her place, when he, suddenly enlightened, springs up and stops her].

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Ah! I understand now.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: What do you understand?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Your secret. Tell me: is it really and truly possible for a woman to love him?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [as if this were beyond all bounds]
sp.p: Well!!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No: answer me. I want to know: I must know. I cant understand it. I can see nothing in him but words, pious resolutions, what people call goodness. You cant love that.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [attempting to snub him by an air of cool propriety]
sp.p: I simply dont know what youre talking about. I dont understand you.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: You do. You lie.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: You do understand; and you know.
Is it possible for a woman to love him?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Yes.
sp.stage: [He covers his face with his hands].
sp.p: Whatever is the matter with you!
sp.stage: [He takes down his hands. Frightened at the tragic mask presented to her, she hurries past him at the utmost possible distance, keeping her eyes on his face until he turns from her and goes to the child's chair beside the hearth, where he sits in the deepest dejection. As she approaches the door, it opens and Burgess enters. Seeing him, she ejaculates]
sp.p: Praise heaven! here's somebody
sp.stage: [and feels safe enough to resume her place at her table. She puts a fresh sheet of paper into the typewriter as Burgess crosses to Eugene].

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [bent on taking care of the distinguished visitor]
sp.p: Well: so this is the way they leave you to yoreself, Mr Morchbanks. Ive come to keep you company.
sp.stage: [Marchbanks looks up at him in consternation, which is quite lost on him].
sp.p: James is receivin a deppitation in the dinin room; and Candy is hupstairs heducating of a young stitcher gurl she's hinterested in.
You must find it lonesome here with no one but the typist to talk to.
sp.stage: [He pulls round the easy chair, and sits down].

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: He'll be all right now that he has the advantage of your polished conversation: thats one comfort, anyhow.
sp.stage: [She begins to typewrite with clattering asperity].

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Hi was not addressin myself to you, young woman, that I'm awerr of.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Did you ever see worse manners, Mr Marchbanks?

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Mr Morchbanks is a gentleman, and knows his place, which is more than some people do.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: It's well you and I are not ladies and gentlemen: I'd talk to you pretty straight if Mr Marchbanks wasnt here.
sp.stage: [She pulls the letter out of the machine so crossly that it tears].
sp.p: There! now I've spoiled this letter! have to be done all over again! Oh, I cant contain myself: silly old fathead!

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Ho! I'm a silly ole fat'ead, am I? Ho, indeed [gasping]! Hall right, my gurl! Hall right. You just wait till I tell that to yore hemployer. Youll see. I'll teach you: see if I dont.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: I—

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: No: youve done it now. No huse a-talking to me. I'll let you know who I am.
sp.stage: [Proserpine shifts her paper carriage with a defiant bang, and disdainfully goes on with her work].
sp.p: Dont you take no notice of her, Mr Morchbanks. She's beneath it.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Hadnt we better change the subject? I—I dont think Miss Garnett meant anything.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Oh, didnt I though, just!

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: I wouldnt demean myself to take notice on her.

div.stage: An electric bell rings twice.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Thats for me.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Oh, we can spare you.
sp.stage: [Somewhat relieved by the triumph of having the last word, and yet half inclined to try to improve on it, he looks after her for a moment; then subsides into his seat by Eugene, and addresses him very confidentially].
sp.p: Now we're alone, Mr Morchbanks, let me give you a friendly int that I wouldnt give to heverybody. Ow long ave you known my son-in-law James ere?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I dont know. I never can remember dates. A few months, perhaps.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Ever notice hennythink queer about him?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I dont think so.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: No more you wouldnt. Thats the danger on it. Well, he's mad.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Mad!

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Mad as a Morch 'are. You take notice on him and youll see.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: But surely that is only because his opinions—

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.stage: [touching him on the knee with his forefinger, and pressing it to hold his attention]
sp.p: Thats the same what I hused to think, Mr Morchbanks. Hi thought long enough that it was ony his opinions; though, mind you, hopinions becomes vurry serious things when people takes to hactin on em as e does. But thats not what I go on.
sp.stage: [He looks round to make sure that they are alone, and bends over to Eugene's ear].
sp.p: What do you think he sez to me this mornin in this very room?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: He sez to me—this is as sure as we're settin here now—he sez ‘I'm a fool,’ he sez; ‘and yore a scounderl.’ Me a scounderl, mind you! And then shook ands with me on it, as if it was to my credit! Do you mean to tell me as that man's sane?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [outside, calling to Proserpine as he opens the door]
sp.p: Get all their names and addresses, Miss Garnett.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Yes, Mr Morell.

div.stage: Morell comes in, with the deputation's documents in his hands.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Yorr he is. Just you keep your heye on im and see.
I'm sorry, James, to ave to make a complaint to you. I dont want to do it; but I feel I oughter, as a matter o right and dooty.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Whats the matter?

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Mr Morchbanks will bear me hout: he was a witness.
Yore young woman so far forgot herself as to call ma a silly old fat'ead.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Oh, now, isnt that exactly like Prossy? She's so frank: she cant contain herself! Poor Prossy! Ha! ha!

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: And do you hexpec me to put up with it from the like of er?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Pooh, nonsense! you cant take any notice of it. Never mind.
sp.stage: [He goes to the cellaret and puts the papers into one of the drawers].

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Oh, Hi dont mind. Hi'm above it. But is it right? thats what I want to know. Is it right?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Thats a question for the Church, not for the laity. Has it done you any harm? thats the question for you, eh? Of course it hasnt. Think no more of it.
sp.stage: [He dismisses the subject by going to his place at the table and setting to work at his correspondence].

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: What did I tell you? Mad as a atter.
sp.stage: [He goes to the table and asks, with the sickly civility of a hungry man]
sp.p: When's dinner, James?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Not for a couple of hours yet.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Gimme a nice book to read over the fire, will you, James: thur's a good chap.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: What sort of book? A good one?

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Nah-oo! Summat pleasant, just to pass the time.
sp.stage: [Morell takes an illustrated paper from the table and offers it. He accepts it humbly].
sp.p: Thank yer, James.
sp.stage: [He goes back to the big chair at the fire, and sits there at his ease, reading].

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Candida will come to entertain you presently. She has got rid of her pupil. She is filling the lamps.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: But that will soil her hands. I cant bear that, Morell: it's a shame. I'll go and fill them.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Youd better not.
She'd only set you to clean my boots, to save me the trouble of doing it myself in the morning.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Dont you keep a servant now, James?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Yes: but she isnt a slave; and the house looks as if I kept three. That means that everyone has to lend a hand. It's not a bad plan: Prossy and I can talk business after breakfast while we're washing up. Washing up's no trouble when there are two people to do it.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Do you think every woman is as coarse-grained as Miss Garnett?

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Thats quite right, Mr Morchbanks: thats quite right. She is corse-grained.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Marchbanks!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Yes?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: How many servants does your father keep?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Oh, I dont know.
sp.stage: [He moves to the sofa, as if to get as far as possible from Morell's questioning, and sits down in great agony of spirit, thinking of the paraffin].

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: So many that you dont know!
When theres anything coarse-grained to be done, you just ring the bell and throw it on to somebody else, eh?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Oh, dont torture me. You dont even ring the bell. But your wife's beautiful fingers are dabbling in paraffin oil while you sit here comfortably preaching about it: everlasting preaching! preaching! words! words! words!

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Har, har! Devil a better!
Ad you there, James, straight.

div.stage: Candida comes in, well aproned, with a reading lamp trimmed, filled, and ready for lighting. She places it on the table near Morell, ready for use.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [brushing her finger tips together with a slight twitch of her nose]
sp.p: If you stay with us, Eugene, I think I will hand over the lamps to you.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I will stay on condition that you hand over all the rough work to me.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Thats very gallant; but I think I should like to see how you do it first.
James: youve not been looking after the house properly.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: What have I done—or not done—my love?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: My own particular pet scrubbing brush has been used for blackleading.
sp.stage: [A heart-breaking wail bursts from Marchbanks. Burgess looks round, amazed. Candida hurries to the sofa].
sp.p: Whats the matter? Are you ill, Eugene?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: No: not ill. Only horror! horror! horror!
sp.stage: [He bows his head on his hands].

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: What! Got the orrors, Mr Morchbanks! Oh, thats bad, at your age. You must leave it off grajally.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Nonsense, papa! It's only poetic horror, isnt it, Eugene [petting him]?

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Oh, poetic orror is it? I beg your pordon, I'm shore.
sp.stage: [He turns to the fire again, deprecating his hasty conclusion].

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: What is it, Eugene? the scrubbing brush?
Well, there! never mind.
Wouldnt you like to present me with a nice new one, with an ivory back inlaid with mother-of-pearl?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [softly and musically, but sadly and longingly]
sp.p: No, not a scrubbing brush, but a boat: a tiny shallop to sail away in, far from the world, where the marble floors are washed by the rain and dried by the sun; where the south wind dusts the beautiful green and purple carpets. Or a chariot! to carry us up into the sky, where the lamps are stars, and dont need to be filled with paraffin oil every day.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: And where there is nothing to do but to be idle, selfish, and useless.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Oh James! how could you spoil it all?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Yes, to be idle, selfish, and useless: that is, to be beautiful and free and happy: hasnt every man desired that with all his soul for the woman he loves? Thats my ideal: whats yours, and that of all the dreadful people who live in these hideous rows of houses? Sermons and scrubbing brushes! With you to preach the sermon and your wife to scrub.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: He cleans the boots, Eugene. You will have to clean them to-morrow for saying that about him.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Oh, dont talk about boots! Your feet should be beautiful on the mountains.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: My feet would not be beautiful on the Hackney Road without boots.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Come, Candy! dont be vulgar. Mr Morchbanks aint accustomed to it. Youre givin him the orrors again. I mean the poetic ones.

div.stage: Morell is silent. Apparently he is busy with his letters: really he is puzzling with misgiving over his new and alarming experience that the surer he is of his moral thrusts, the more swiftly and effectively Eugene parries them. To find himself beginning to fear a man whom he does not respect afflicts him bitterly. Miss Garnett comes in with a telegram.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Reply paid. The boy's waiting.
sp.stage: [To Candida, coming back to her machine and sitting down]
sp.p: Maria is ready for you now in the kitchen, Mrs Morell
The onions have come.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Onions!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Yes, onions. Not even Spanish ones: nasty little red onions. You shall help me to slice them. Come along.

div.stage: She catches him by the wrist and runs out, pulling him after her. Burgess rises in consternation, and stands aghast on the hearth-rug, staring after them.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Candy didnt oughter andle a hearl's nevvy like that. It's goin too fur with it. Lookee ere, James: do e often git taken queer like that?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I dont know.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: He talks very pretty. I awlus had a turn for a bit of poetry. Candy takes arter me that-a-way. Huseter make me tell er fairy stories when she was only a little kiddy not that igh
sp.stage: [indicating a stature of two feet or thereabouts].

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Ah, indeed.
sp.stage: [He blots the telegram and goes out].

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Used you to make the fairy stories up out of your own head?

div.stage: Burgess, not deigning to reply, strikes an attitude of the haughtiest disdain on the hearth-rug.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: I should never have supposed you had it in you. By the way, I'd better warn you, since youve taken such a fancy to Mr Marchbanks. He's mad.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Mad! What! Im too!!

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Mad as a March hare. He did frighten me, I can tell you, just before you came in that time. Havnt you noticed the queer things he says?

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: So thats what the poetic orrors means. Blame me if it didnt come into my ed once or twyst that he was a bit horff is chump!
sp.stage: [He crosses the room to the door, lifting up his voice as he goes].
sp.p: Well, this is a pretty sort of asylum for a man to be in, with no one but you to take care of him!

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Yes, what a dreadful thing it would be if anything happened to you!

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Dont you haddress no remorks to me. Tell your hemployer that Ive gone into the gorden for a smoke.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Oh!

div.stage: Before Burgess can retort, Morell comes back.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Goin for a turn in the gording to smoke, James.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Oh, all right, all right.
sp.stage: [Burgess goes out pathetically in the character of a weary old man. Morell stands at the table, turning over his papers, and adding, across to Proserpine, half humorously, half absently]
sp.p: Well, Miss Prossy, why have you been calling my father-in-law names?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.stage: [blushing fiery red, and looking quickly up at him, half scared, half reproachful]
sp.p: I—

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [with tender gaiety, leaning across the table towards her, and consoling her]
sp.p: Oh, come! come! come! Never mind, Pross: he is a silly old fathead, isnt he?

div.stage: With an explosive sob, she makes a dash at the door, and vanishes, banging it. Morell, shaking his head resignedly, sighs, and goes wearily to his chair, where he sits down and sets to work, looking old and careworn. Candida comes in. She has finished her household work and taken off the apron. She at once notices his dejected appearance, and posts herself quietly at the visitors' chair, looking down at him attentively. She says nothing.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [looking up, but with his pen raised ready to resume his work]
sp.p: Well? Where is Eugene?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Washing his hands in the scullery under the tap. He will make an excellent cook if he can only get over his dread of Maria.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Ha! No doubt.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [going nearer, and putting her hand down softly on his to stop him as she says]
