sp.p: Come here, dear. Let me look at you.
sp.stage: [He drops his pen and yields himself to her disposal. She makes him rise, and brings him a little away from the table, looking at him critically all the time].
sp.p: Turn your face to the light.
My boy is not looking well. Has he been overworking?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Nothing more than usual.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: He looks very pale, and grey, and wrinkled, and old.
sp.stage: [His melancholy deepens: and she attacks it with wilful gaiety]
sp.p: Here:
youve done enough writing for today. Leave Prossy to finish it. Come and talk to me.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: But—

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Yes, I must be talked to.
sp.stage: [She makes him sit down, and seats herself on the carpet beside his knee].
sp.p: Now

youre beginning to look better already. Why must you go out every night lecturing and talking? I hardly have one evening a week with you. Of course what you say is all very true; but it does no good: they dont mind what you say to them one little bit. They think they agree with you; but whats the use of their agreeing with you if they go and do just the opposite of what you tell them the moment your back is turned? Look at our congregation at St Dominic's! Why do they come to hear you talking about Christianity every Sunday? Why, just because theyve been so full of business and money-making for six days that they want to forget all about it and have a rest on the seventh; so that they can go back fresh and make money harder than ever! You positively help them at it instead of hindering them.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: You know very well, Candida, that I often blow them up soundly for that. And if there is nothing in their churchgoing but rest and diversion, why dont they try something more amusing? more self-indulgent? There must be some good in the fact that they prefer St Dominic's to worse places on Sundays.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Oh, the worse places arnt open; and even if they were, they darent be seen going to them. Besides, James dear, you preach so splendidly that it's as good as a play for them. Why do you think the women are so enthusiastic?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Candida!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
MORELL.
sp.p: Prossy's complaint! What do you mean, Candida?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Yes, Prossy, and all the other secretaries you ever had. Why does Prossy condescend to wash up the things, and to peel potatoes and abase herself in all manner of ways for six shillings a week less than she used to get in a city office? She's in love with you, James: thats the reason. Theyre all in love with you. And you are in love with preaching because you do it so beautifully. And you think it's all enthusiasm for the kingdom of Heaven on earth; and so do they. You dear silly!

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Candida: what dreadful! what soul-destroying cynicism! Are you jesting? Or—can it be?—are you jealous?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Yes, I feel a little jealous sometimes.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Of Prossy?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: No, no, no, no. Not jealous of anybody. Jealous for somebody else, who is not loved as he ought to be.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Me?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: You! Why, youre spoiled with love and worship: you get far more than is good for you. No: I mean Eugene.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Eugene!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: It seems unfair that all the love should go to you, and none to him; although he needs it so much more than you do.
sp.stage: [A convulsive movement shakes him in spite of himself].
sp.p: Whats the matter? Am I worrying you?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Not at all.
You know that I have perfect confidence in you, Candida.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: You vain thing! Are you so sure of your irresistible attractions?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Candida: you are shocking me. I never thought of my attractions. I thought of your goodness, of your purity. That is what I confide in.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: What a nasty uncomfortable thing to say to me! Oh, you are a clergyman, James: a thorough clergyman!

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: So Eugene says.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [with lively interest, leaning over to him with her arms on his knee]
sp.p: Eugene's always right. He's a wonderful boy: I have grown fonder and fonder of him all the time I was away. Do you know, James, that though he has not the least suspicion of it himself, he is ready to fall madly in love with me?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Oh, he has no suspicion of it himself, hasnt he?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Not a bit.
sp.stage: [She takes her arms from his knee, and turns thoughtfully, sinking into a more restful attitude with her hands in her lap].
sp.p: Some day he will know: when he is grown up and experienced, like you. And he will know that I must have known. I wonder what he will think of me then.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: No evil, Candida. I hope and trust, no evil.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: That will depend.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Depend!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Yes: it wiil depend on what happens to him.
Dont you see? It will depend on how he comes to learn what love really is. I mean on the sort of woman who will teach it to him.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Yes. No. I dont know what you mean.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: If he learns it from a good woman, then it will be all right: he will forgive me.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Forgive?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: But suppose he learns it from a bad woman, as so many men do, especially poetic men, who imagine all women are angels! Suppose he only discovers the value of love when he has thrown it away and degraded himself in his ignorance! Will he forgive me then, do you think?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Forgive you for what?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [realizing how stupid he is, and a little disappointed, though quite tenderly so]
sp.p: Dont you understand?
sp.stage: [He shakes his head. She turns to him again, so as to explain with the fondest intimacy].
sp.p: I mean, will he forgive me for not teaching him myself? For abandoning him to the bad women for the sake of my goodness, of my purity, as you call it? Ah, James, how little you understand me, to talk of your confidence in my goodness and purity! I would give them both to poor Eugene as willingly as I would give my shawl to a beggar dying of cold, if there were nothing else to restrain me. Put your trust in my love for you, James; for if that went, I should care very little for your sermons: mere phrases that you cheat yourself and others with every day.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: His words!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [checking herself quickly in the act of getting up]
sp.p: Whose words?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Eugene's.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: He is always right. He understands you; he understands me; he understands Prossy; and you, darling, you understand nothing.
sp.stage: [She laughs, and kisses him to console him. He recoils as if stabbed, and springs up].

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: How can you bear to do that when—Oh, Candida
I had rather you had plunged a grappling iron into my heart than given me that kiss.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: My dear: whats the matter?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Dont touch me.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: James!!!

div.stage: They are interrupted by the entrance of Marchbanks with Burgess, who stop near the door, staring.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Is anything the matter?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [deadly white, putting an iron constraint on himself]
sp.p: Nothing but this: that either you were right this morning, or Candida is mad.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: What! Candy mad too! Oh, come! come! come!
sp.stage: [He crosses the room to the fireplace, protesting as he goes, and knocks the ashes out of his pipe on the bars].

div.stage: Morell sits down at his table desperately, leaning forward to hide his face, and interlacing his fingers rigidly to keep them steady.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Oh, youre only shocked! Is that all? How conventional all you unconventional people are!
sp.stage: [She sits gaily on the arm of the chair].

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Come: be'ave yourself, Candy. Whatll Mr Morchbanks think of you?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: This comes of James teaching me to think for myself, and never to hold back out of fear of what other people may think of me. It works beautifully as long as I think the same things as he does. But now! because I have just thought something different! look at him! Just look!

div.stage: Eugene looks, and instantly presses his hand on his heart, as if some pain had shot through it. He sits down on the sofa like a man witnessing a tragedy.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Well, James, you certnly haint as himpressive lookin as usu'l.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [with a laugh which is half a sob]
sp.p: I suppose not. I beg all your pardons: I was not conscious of making a fuss.
Well, well, well, well, well!
sp.stage: [He sets to work at his papers again with resolute cheerfulness].

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [going to the sofa and sitting beside Marchbanks, still in a bantering humor]
sp.p: Well, Eugene: why are you so sad? Did the onions make you cry?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: It is your cruelty. I hate cruelty. It is a horrible thing to see one person make another suffer.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Poor boy! have I been cruel? Did I make it slice nasty little red onions?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Oh, stop, stop: I dont mean myself. You have made him suffer frightfully. I feel his pain in my own heart. I know that it is not your fault: it is something that must happen; but dont make light of it. I shudder when you torture him and laugh.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: I torture James! Nonsense, Eugene: how you exaggerate! Silly!
sp.stage: [She rises and goes to the table, a little troubled].
sp.p: Dont work any more, dear. Come and talk to us.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Ah no: I cant talk. I can only preach.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Well, come and preach.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Aw no, Candy. Ang it all!

div.stage: Lexy Mill comes in, anxious and important.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: How do you do, Mrs Morell? So glad to see you back again.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Thank you, Lexy. You know Eugene, dont you?

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: Oh yes. How do you do, Marchbanks?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Quite well, thanks.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: lve just come from the Guild of St Matthew. They are in the greatest consternation about your telegram.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: What did you telegraph about, James?

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: He was to have spoken for them tonight. Theyve taken the large hall in Mare Street and spent a lot of money on posters. Morell's telegram was to say he couldnt come. It came on them like a thunderbolt.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [surprised, and beginning to suspect something wrong]
sp.p: Given up an engagement to speak!

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Fust time in his life, I'll bet. Aint it, Candy?

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: They decided to send an urgent telegram to you asking whether you could not change your mind. Have you received it?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Yes, yes: I got it.

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: It was reply paid.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Yes, I know. I answered it. I cant go.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: But why, James?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Because I dont choose. These people forget that I am a man: they think I am a talking machine to be turned on for their pleasure every evening of my life. May I not have one night at home, with my wife, and my friends?

div.stage: They are all amazed at this outburst, except Eugene. His expression remains unchanged.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Oh, James, you mustnt mind what I said about that. And if you dont go youll have an attack of bad conscience tomorrow.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: I know, of course, that they make the most unreasonable demands on you. But they have been telegraphing all over the place for another speaker; and they can get nobody but the President of the Agnostic League.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Well, an excellent man. What better do they want?

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: But he always insists so powerfully on the divorce of Socialism from Christianity. He will undo all the good we have been doing. Of course you know best; but—
sp.stage: [he shrugs his shoulders and wanders to the hearth beside Burgess].

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Oh, do go, James. We'll all go.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Look ere, Candy! I say! Lets stay at home by the fire, comfortable. He wont need to be more'n a couple-o-hour away.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Youll be just as comfortable at the meeting. We'll all sit on the platform and be great people.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Oh please dont let us go on the platform. No: everyone will stare at us: I couldnt. I'll sit at the back of the room.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Dont be afraid. Theyll be too busy looking at James to notice you.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Prossy's complaint, Candida! Eh?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Yes: Prossy's complaint.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Prossy's complaint! What are you talkin about, James?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [not heeding him, rises; goes to the door; and holds it open, calling in a commanding tone]
sp.p: Miss Garnett.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Yes, Mr Morell. Coming.

div.stage: They all wait, except Burgess, who turns stealthily to Lexy.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Listen ere, Mr Mill. Whats Prossy's complaint? Whats wrong with er?

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Well, I dont exactly know; but she spoke very strangely to me this morning. I'm afraid she's a little out of her mind sometimes.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Why, it must be catchin! Four in the same ouse!

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: What is it, Mr Morell?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Telegraph to the Guild of St Matthew that I am coming.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Dont they expect you?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Do as I tell you.

div.stage: Proserpine, frightened, sits down at her typewriter, and obeys. Morell, now unaccountably resolute and forceful, goes across to Burgess. Candida watches his movements with growing wonder and misgiving.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Burgess: you dont want to come.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Oh, dont put it like that, James. It's ony that it aim Sunday, you know.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: I'm sorry. I thought you might like to be introduced to the chairman. He's on the Works Committee of the County Council, and has some influence in the matter of contracts.
Youll come?

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Cawrse I'll come, James. Aint it awlus a pleasure to ear you!

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I shall want you to take some notes at the meeting, Miss Garnett, if you have no other engagement.
You are coming, Lexy, I suppose?

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: Certainly.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: We're all coming, James.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: No: you are not coming; and Eugene is not coming. You will stay here and entertain him—to celebrate your return home.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: But, James—

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I insist. You do not want to come; and he does not want to come.
Oh, dont concern yourselves: I shall have plenty of people without you: your chairs will be wanted by unconverted people who have never heard me before.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Eugene: wouldn't you like to come?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: I should be afraid to let myself go before Eugene: he is so critical of sermons.
He knows I am afraid of him: he told me as much this morning. Well, I shall shew him how much afraid I am by leaving him here in your custody, Candida.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Thats brave. Thats beautiful.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: But—but—Is anything the matter, James?
I cant understand—

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [taking her tenderly in his arms and kissing her on the forehead]
sp.p: Ah, I thought it was I who couldnt understand, dear.

div.head: ACT III
div.stage: Past ten in the evening. The curtains are drawn, and the lamps lighted. The typewriter is in its case: the large table has been cleared and tidied: everything indicates that the day's work is over. Candida and Marchbanks are sitting by the fire. The reading lamp is on the mantelshelf above Marchbanks, who is in the small chair, reading aloud. A little pile of manuscripts and a couple of volumes of poetry are on the carpet beside him. Candida is in the easy chair. The poker, a light brass one, is upright in her hand. Leaning back and looking intently at the point of it, with her feet stretched towards the blaze, she is in a waking dream, miles away from the surroundings and completely oblivious of Eugene.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Every poet that ever lived has put that thought into a sonnet. He must: he cant help it.
sp.stage: [He looks to her for assent, and notices her absorption in the poker].
sp.p: Havnt you been listening?
Mrs Morell!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Eh?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Havnt you been listening?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Oh yes. It's very nice. Go on, Eugene. I'm longing to hear what happens to the angel.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [letting the manuscript drop from his hand to the floor]
sp.p: I beg your pardon for boring you.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: But you are not boring me, I assure you. Please go on. Do, Eugene.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I finished the poem about the angel quarter of an hour ago. Ive read you several things since.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: I'm so sorry, Eugene. I think the poker must have hypnotized me.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: It made me horribly uneasy.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Why didnt you tell me? I'd have put it down at once.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I was afraid of making you uneasy too. It looked as if it were a weapon. If I were a hero of old I should have laid my drawn sword between us. If Morell had come in he would have thought you had taken up the poker because there was no sword between us.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: What?
I cant quite follow that. Those sonnets of yours have perfectly addled me. Why should there be a sword between us?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Oh, never mind.
sp.stage: [He stoops to pick up the manuscript].

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Put that down again, Eugene. There are limits to my appetite for poetry: even your poetry. Youve been reading to me for more than two hours, ever since James went out. I want to talk.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No: I mustnt talk.
sp.stage: [He looks round him in his lost way, and adds, suddenly]
sp.p: I think I'll go out and take a walk in the park.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Nonsense: it's closed long ago. Come and sit down on the hearth-rug, and talk moonshine as you usually do. I want to be amused. Dont you want to?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Then come along.
sp.stage: [She moves her chair back a little to make room].

div.stage: He hesitates; then timidly stretches himself on the hearth-rug, face upwards, and throws back his head across her knees, looking up at her.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Oh, Ive been so miserable all the evening, because I was doing right. Now I'm doing wrong; and I'm happy.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Yes: I'm sure you feel a great grown-up wicked deceiver. Quite proud of yourself, arnt you?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [raising his head quickly and turning a little to look round at her]
sp.p: Take care. I'm ever so much older than you, if you only knew.
sp.stage: [He turns quite over on his knees, with his hands clasped and his arms on her lap, and speaks with growing impulse, his blood beginning to stir].
sp.p: May I say some wicked things to you?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [without the least fear or coldness, and with perfect respect for his passion, but with a touch of her wise-hearted maternal humor]
sp.p: No. But you may say anything you really and truly feel. Anything at all, no matter what it is. I am not afraid, so long as it is your real self that speaks, and not a mere attitude: a gallant attitude, or a wicked attitude, or even a poetic attitude. I put you on your honor and truth. Now say whatever you want to.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [the eager expression vanishing utterly from his lips and nostrils as his eyes light up with pathetic spirituality]
sp.p: Oh, now I cant say anything: all the words I know belong to some attitude or other—all except one.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: What one is that?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [softly, losing himself in the music of the name]
sp.p: Candida, Candida, Candida, Candida, Candida. I must say that now, because you have put me on my honor and truth; and I never think or feel Mrs Morell: it is always Candida.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Of course. And what have you to say to Candida?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Nothing but to repeat your name a thousand times. Dont you feel that every time is a prayer to you?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Doesnt it make you happy to be able to pray?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Yes, very happy.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Well, that happiness is the answer to your prayer. Do you want anything more?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: No: I have come into Heaven, where want is unknown.

div.stage: Morell comes in. He halts on the threshold, and takes in the scene at a glance.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I hope I dont disturb you.

div.stage: Candida starts up violently, but without the smallest embarrassment, laughing at herself. Eugene, capsized by her sudden movement, recovers himself without rising, and sits on the rug hugging his ankles, also quite unembarrassed.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Oh, James, how you startled me! I was so taken up with Eugene that I didnt hear your latchkey. How did the meeting go off? Did you speak well?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: I have never spoken better in my life.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: That was first rate! How much was the collection?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: I forgot to ask.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: He must have spoken splendidly, or he would never have forgotten that.
Where are all the others?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: They left long before I could get away: I thought I should never escape. I believe they are having supper somewhere.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Oh, in that case, Maria may go to bed. I'll tell her.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [squatting grotesquely on the hearth-rug, and actually at ease with Morell: even impishly humorous]
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Have you anything to tell me?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Only that I have been making a fool of myself here in private whilst you have been making a fool of yourself in public.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Hardly in the same way, I think.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: The very, very, very same way. I have been playing the Good Man. Just like you. When you began your heroics about leaving me here with Candida—

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Candida!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Oh yes: Ive got that far. But dont be afraid. Heroics are infectious: I caught the disease from you. I swore not to say a word in your absence that I would not not have said a month ago in your presence.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Did you keep your oath?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [suddenly perching himself on the back of the easy chair]
sp.p: It kept itself somehow until about ten minutes ago. Up to that moment I went on desperately reading to her—reading my own poems—anybody's poems—to stave off a conversation. I was standing outside the gate of Heaven, and refusing to go in. Oh, you cant think how heroic it was, and how uncomfortable! Then—

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Then?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [prosaically slipping down into a quite ordinary attitude on the seat of the chair]
sp.p: Then she couldnt bear being read to any longer.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: And you approached the gate of Heaven at last?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Well?
Speak, man: have you no feeling for me?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Then she became an angel; and there was a flaming sword that turned every way, so that I couldnt go in; for I saw that that gate was really the gate of Hell.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: She repulsed you!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No, you fool: if she had done that I should never have seen that I was in Heaven already. Repulsed me! You think that would have saved us! virtuous indignation! Oh, you are not worthy to live in the same world with her.
sp.stage: [He turns away contemptuously to the other side of the room].

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [who has watched him quietly without changing his place]
sp.p: Do you think you make yourself more worthy by reviling me, Eugene?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Here endeth the thousand and first lesson. Morell: I dont think much of your preaching after all: I believe I could do it better myself. The man I want to meet is the man that Candida married.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: The man that—? Do you mean me?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I dont mean the Reverend James Mavor Morell, moralist and windbag. I mean the real man that the Reverend James must have hidden somewhere inside his black coat: the man that Candida loved. You cant make a woman like Candida love you by merely buttoning your collar at the back instead of in front.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: When Candida promised to marry me, I was the same moralist and windbag you now see. I wore my black coat; and my collar was buttoned behind instead of in front. Do you think she would have loved me any the better for being insincere in my profession?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Oh, she forgave you, just as she forgives me for being a coward, and a weakling, and what you call a snivelling little whelp and all the rest of it.
A woman like that has divine insight: she loves our souls, and not our follies and vanities and illusions, nor our collars and coats, nor any other of the rags and tatters we are rolled up in.
sp.stage: [He reflects on this for an instant: then turns intently to question Morell].
sp.p: What I want to know is how you got past the flaming sword that stopped me.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Perhaps because I was not interrupted at the end of ten minutes.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: What!

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Man can climb to the highest summits; but he cannot dwell there long.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: It's false: there can he dwell for ever, and there only. It's in the other moments that he can find no rest, no sense of the silent glory of life. Where would you have me spend my moments, if not on the summits?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: In the scullery, slicing onions and filling lamps.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Or in the pulpit, scrubbing cheap earthenware souls?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Yes, that too. It was there that I earned my golden moment, and the right, in that moment, to ask her to love me. I did not take the moment on credit; nor did I use it to steal another man's happiness.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [rather disgustedly, trotting back towards the fireplace]
sp.p: I have no doubt you conducted the transaction as honestly as if you were buying a pound of cheese.
sp.stage: [He stops on the brink of the hearth-rug, and adds, thoughtfully, to himself, with his back turned to Morell]
sp.p: I could only go to her as a beggar.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: A beggar dying of cold! asking for her shawl!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Thank you for touching up my poetry. Yes, if you like: a beggar dying of cold, asking for her shawl.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: And she refused. Shall I tell you why she refused? I can tell you, on her own authority. It was because of—

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: She didnt refuse.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Not!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: She offered me all I chose to ask for: her shawl, her wings, the wreath of stars on her head, the lilies in her hand, the crescent moon beneath her feet—

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Out with the truth, man: my wife is my wife: I want no more of your poetic fripperies. I know well that if I have lost her love and you have gained it, no law will bind her.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Catch me by the shirt collar, Morell: she will arrange it for me afterwards as she did this morning.
I shall feel her hands touch me.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: You young imp, do you know how dangerous it is to say that to me? Or
has something made you brave?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I'm not afraid now. I disliked you before: that was why I shrank from your touch. But I saw today—when she tortured you—that you love her. Since then I have been your friend: you may strangle me if you like.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Eugene: if that is not a heartless lie—if you have a spark of human feeling left in you—will you tell me what has happened during my absence?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: What happened! Why, the flaming sword
—Well, in plain prose, I loved her so exquisitely that I wanted nothing more than the happiness of being in such love. And before I had time to come down from the highest summits, you came in.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: So it is still unsettled. Still the misery of doubt.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Misery! I am the happiest of men. I desire nothing now but her happiness.

Oh, Morell, let us both give her up. Why should she have to choose between a wretched little nervous disease like me, and a pig-headed parson like you? Let us go on a pilgrimage, you to the east and I to the west, in search of a worthy lover for her: some beautiful archangel with purple wings—

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Some fiddlestick! Oh, if she is mad enough to leave me for you, who will protect her? who will help her? who will work for her? who will be a father to her children?
sp.stage: [He sits down distractedly on the sofa, with his elbows on his knees and his head propped on his clenched fists].

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: She does not ask those silly questions. It is she who wants somebody to protect, to help, to work for: somebody to give her children to protect, to help and to work for. Some grown up man who has become as a little child again. Oh, you fool, you fool, you triple fool! I am the man, Morell: I am the man.
You dont understand what a woman is. Send for her, Morell: send for her and let her choose between—
sp.stage: [The door opens and Candida enters. He stops as if petrified].

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: What on earth are you at, Eugene?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: James and I are having a preaching match; and he is getting the worst of it.

div.stage: Candida looks quickly round at Morell. Seeing that he is distressed, she hurries down to him, greatly vexed.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: You have been annoying him. Now I wont have it, Eugene: do you hear?
sp.stage: [She puts her hand on Morell's shoulder, and quite forgets her wifely tact in her anger].
sp.p: My boy shall not be worried: I will protect him.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Protect!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: What have you been saying?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Nothing. I—

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Eugene! Nothing?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: I mean—I—I'm very sorry. I wont do it again: indeed I wont. I'll let him alone.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [indignantly, with an aggressive movement towards Eugene]
sp.p: Let me alone! You young—

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Sh!—no: let me deal with him, James.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Oh, youre not angry with me, are you?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Yes I am: very angry. I have a good mind to pack you out of the house.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [taken aback by Candida's vigor, and by no means relishing the position of being rescued by her from another man]
sp.p: Gently, Candida, gently. I am able to take care of myself.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Yes, dear: of course you are. But you musnt be annoyed and made miserable.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [almost in tears, turning to the door]
sp.p: I'll go.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Oh, you neednt go: I cant turn you out at this time of night.
Shame on you! For shame!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: But what have I done?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: I know what you have done: as well as if I had been here all the time. Oh, it was unworthy! You are like a child: you cannot hold your tongue.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I would die ten times over sooner than give you a moment's pain.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Much good your dying would do me!

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Candida, my dear: this altercation is hardly quite seemly. It is a matter between two men; and I am the right person to settle it.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Two men! Do you call that a man!
You bad boy!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [gathering a whimsically affectionate courage from the scolding]
sp.p: If I am to be scolded like a boy, I must make a boy's excuse. He began it. And he's bigger than I am.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [losing confidence a little as her concern for Morell's dignity takes the alarm]
sp.p: That cant be true.
You didnt begin it, James, did you?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: You began it: this morning.
sp.stage: [Candida, instantly connecting this with his mysterious allusion in the afternoon to something told him by Eugene in the morning, looks at him with quick suspicion. Morell proceeds, with the emphasis of offended superiority]
sp.p: But your other point is true. I am certainly the bigger of the two, and, I hope, the stronger, Candida. So you had better leave the matter in my hands.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Yes, dear; but—
I dont understand about this morning.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: You need not understand, my dear.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: But James, I
—Oh bother! Here they all come.
sp.stage: [She goes out to let them in].

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Oh, Morell, isnt it dreadful? She's angry with us: she hates me. What shall I do?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [with quaint desperation, walking up and down the middle of the room]
sp.p: Eugene: my head is spinning round. I shall begin to laugh presently.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No, no: she'll think Ive thrown you into hysterics. Dont laugh.

div.stage: Boisterous voices and laughter are heard approaching. Lexy Mill, his eyes sparkling, and his bearing denoting unwonted elevation of spirit, enters with Burgess, who is greasy and self-complacent, but has all his wits about him. Miss Garnett, with her smartest hat and jacket on, follows them; but though her eyes are brighter than before, she is evidently a prey to misgiving. She places herself with her back to her typewriting table, with one hand on it to steady herself, passing the other across her forehead as if she were a little tired and giddy. Marchbanks relapses into shyness and edges away into the corner near the window, where Morell's books are.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Morell: I must congratulate you.
What a noble, splendid, inspired address you gave us! You surpassed yourself.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: So you did, James. It fair kep me awake to the lars' word. Didnt it, Miss Gornett?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Oh, I wasnt minding you: I was trying to make notes.
sp.stage: [She takes out her note-book, and looks at her stenography, which nearly makes her cry].

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Did I go too fast, Pross?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Much too fast. You know I cant do more than ninety words a minute.
sp.stage: [She relieves her feelings by throwing her note-book angrily beside her machine, ready for use next morning].

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Oh well, well, never mind, never mind, never mind. Have you all had supper?

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: Mr Burgess has been kind enough to give us a really splendid supper at the Belgrave.

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Dont mention it, Mr Mill.
Youre arty welcome to my little treat.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: We had champagne. I never tasted it before. I feel quite giddy.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: A champagne supper! That was very handsome. Was it my eloquence that produced all this extravagance?

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Your eloquence, and Mr Burgess's goodness of heart.
And what a very fine fellow the chairman is, Morell! He came to supper with us.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [with long drawn significance, looking at Burgess]
sp.p: O-o-o-h! the chairman. Now I understand.

div.stage: Burgess covers with a deprecatory cough a lively satisfaction with his own diplomatic cunning. Lexy folds his arms and leans against the head of the sofa in a high-spirited attitude after nearly losing his balance. Candida comes in with glasses, lemons, and a jug of hot water on a tray.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Who will have some lemonade? You know our rules: total abstinence.
sp.stage: [She puts the tray on the table, and takes up the lemon squeezer, looking enquiringly round at them].

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: No use, dear. Theyve all had champagne. Pross has broken her pledge.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: You dont mean to say youve been drinking champagne!

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE
sp.p: Yes I do. I'm only a beer teetotaller, not a champagne teetotaller. I dont like beer. Are there any letters for me to answer, Mr Morell?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: No more tonight.

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: Very well. Goodnight, everybody.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: Had I not better see you home, Miss Garnett?

sp.speaker: PROSERPINE.
sp.p: No thank you. I shant trust myself with anybody tonight. I wish I hadnt taken any of that stuff.
sp.stage: [She takes uncertain aim at the door; dashes at it; and barely escapes without disaster].

sp.speaker: BURGESS
sp.p: Stuff indeed! That gurl dunno what champagne is! Pommery and Greeno at twelve and six a bottle. She took two glasses amost straight horff.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Go and look after her, Lexy.

sp.speaker: LEXY
sp.p: But if she should really be—Suppose she began to sing in the street, or anything of that sort.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Just so: she may. Thats why youd better see her safely home.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Do, Lexy: theres a good fellow.
sp.stage: [She shakes his hand and pushes him gently to the door].

sp.speaker: LEXY.
sp.p: It's evidently my duty to go. I hope it may not be necessary. Goodnight, Mrs Morell.
Goodnight.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: He was gushin with hextra piety hisself arter two sips. People carnt drink like they huseter.
Well, James: it's time to lock up. Mr Morchbanks: shall I ave the pleasure of your company for a bit o the way ome?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Yes: I'd better go.
sp.stage: [He hurries towards the door; but Candida places herself before it, barring his way].

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: You sit down. Youre not going yet.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No: I—I didnt mean to.
sp.stage: [He sits down abjectly on the sofa].

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Mr Marchbanks will stay the night with us, papa.

sp.speaker: BURGESS.
sp.p: Oh well, I'll say goodnight. So long, James.
sp.stage: [He shakes hands with Morell, and goes over to Eugene].
sp.p: Make em give you a nightlight by your bed, Mr Morchbanks: itll comfort you if you wake up in the night with a touch of that complaint of yores. Goodnight.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Thank you: I will. Goodnight, Mr Burgess.
sp.stage: [They shake hands. Burgess goes to the door].

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Stay here, dear: I'll put on papa's coat for him.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Morell: theres going to be a terrible scene. Arnt you afraid?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Not in the least.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I never envied you your courage before.
sp.stage: [He puts his hand appealingly on Morell's forearm].
sp.p: Stand by me, wont you?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Each for himself, Eugene. She must choose between us now.

div.stage: Candida returns. Eugene creeps back to the sofa like a guilty schoolboy.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Are you sorry?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Yes. Heartbroken.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Well, then, you are forgiven. Now go off to bed like a good little boy: I want to talk to James about you.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Oh, I cant do that, Morell. I must be here. I'll not go away. Tell her.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Tell me what?
sp.stage: [His eyes avoid hers furtively. She turns and mutely transfers the question to Morell].

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I have nothing to tell her, except
sp.stage: [here his voice deepens to a measured and mournful tenderness]
sp.p: that she is my greatest treasure on earth—if she is really mine.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [coldly, offended by his yielding to his orator's instinct and treating her as if she were the audience at the Guild of St Matthew]
sp.p: I am sure Eugene can say no less, if that is all.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Morell: she's laughing at us.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: There is nothing to laugh at. Are you laughing at us, Candida?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Eugene is very quick-witted, James. I hope I am going to laugh; but I am not sure that I am not going to be very angry.
sp.stage: [She goes to the fireplace, and stands there leaning with her arm on the mantelpiece, and her foot on the fender, whilst Eugene steals to Morell and plucks him by the sleeve].

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Stop, Morell. Dont let us say anything.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [pushing Eugene away without deigning to look at him]
sp.p: I hope you dont mean that as a threat, Candida.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Take care, James. Eugene: I asked you to go. Are you going?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: He shall not go. I wish him to remain.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I'll go. I'll do whatever you want.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Stop!
Didnt you hear James say he wished you to stay? James is master here. Dont you know that?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [flushing with a young poet's rage against tyranny]
sp.p: By what right is he master?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Tell him, James.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: My dear: I dont know of any right that makes me master. I assert no such right.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: You dont know! Oh, James! James!
I wonder do you understand, Eugene!
sp.stage: [He shakes his head helplessly, not daring to look at her].
sp.p: No: youre too young. Well, I give you leave to stay: to stay and learn.
sp.stage: [She comes away from the hearth and places herself between them].
sp.p: Now, James! whats the matter? Come: tell me.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Dont.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Come. Out with it!

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I meant to prepare your mind carefully, Candida, so as to prevent misunderstanding.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Yes, dear: I am sure you did. But never mind: I shant misunderstand.

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: Well—er—
sp.stage: [he hesitates, unable to find the long explanation which he supposed to be available].

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Eugene declares that you are in love with him.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No, no, no, no, never. I did not, Mrs Morell: it's not true. I said I loved you. I said I understood you, and that he couldnt. And it was not after what passed there before the fire that I spoke: it was not, on my word. It was this morning.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: This morning!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Yes.
sp.stage: [He looks at her, pleading for credence, and then adds simply]
sp.p: That was what was the matter with my collar.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Your collar?
sp.stage: [Suddenly taking in his meaning she turns to Morell, shocked].
sp.p: Oh, James: did you—[she stops]?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: You know, Candida, that I have a temper to struggle with. And he said
that you despised me in your heart.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Did you say that?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Then James has just told me a falsehood. Is that what you mean?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: No, no: I—I—
it was David's wife. And it wasnt at home: it was when she saw him dancing before all the people.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [taking the cue with a debater's adroitness]
sp.p: Dancing before all the people, Candida; and thinking he was moving their hearts by his mission when they were only suffering from—Prossy's complaint.
sp.stage: [She is about to protest: he raises his hand to silence her].
sp.p: Dont try to look indignant, Candida—

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Try!

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Eugene was right. As you told me a few hours after, he is always right. He said nothing that you did not say far better yourself. He is the poet, who sees everything; and I am the poor parson, who understands nothing.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Do you mind what is said by a foolish boy, because I said something like it in jest?

sp.speaker: MORELL.
sp.p: That foolish boy can speak with the inspiration of a child and the cunning of a serpent. He has claimed that you belong to him and not to me; and, rightly or wrongly, I have come to fear that it may be true. I will not go about tortured with doubts and suspicions. I will not live with you and keep a secret from you. I will not suffer the intolerable degradation of jealousy. We have agreed—he and I—that you shall choose between us now. I await your decision.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.stage: [slowly recoiling a step, her heart hardened by his rhetoric in spite of the sincere feeling behind it]
sp.p: Oh! I am to choose am I? I suppose it is quite settled that I must belong to one or the other.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Quite. You must choose definitely.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Morell: you dont understand. She means that she belongs to herself.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: I mean that, and a good deal more, Master Eugene, as you will both find out presently. And pray, my lords and masters, what have you to offer for my choice? I am up for auction, it seems. What do you bid, James?

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Cand—
sp.stage: [He breaks down: his eyes and throat fill with tears: the orator becomes a wounded animal].
sp.p: I cant speak—

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Ah, dearest—

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Stop: it's not fair. You mustnt shew her that you suffer, Morell. I am on the rack too; but I am not crying.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Yes: you are right. It is not for pity that I am bidding.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: I beg your pardon, James: I did not mean to touch you. I am waiting to hear your bid.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: I have nothing to offer you but my strength for your defence, my honesty for your surety, my ability and industry for your livelihood, and my authority and position for your dignity. That is all it becomes a man to offer to a woman.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: And you, Eugene? What do you offer?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: My weakness. My desolation. My heart's need.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Thats a good bid, Eugene. Now I know how to make my choice.

div.stage: She pauses and looks curiously from one to the other, as if weighing them. Morell, whose lofty confidence has changed into heart-breaking dread at Eugene's bid, loses all power of concealing his anxiety. Eugene, strung to the highest tension, does not move a muscle.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [in a suffocated voice: the appeal bursting from the depths of his anguish]
sp.p: Candida!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Coward!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: I give myself to the weaker of the two.

div.stage: Eugene divines her meaning at once: his face whitens like steel in a furnace.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [bowing his head with the calm of collapse]
sp.p: I accept your sentence, Candida.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Do you understand, Eugene?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: Oh, I feel I'm lost. He cannot bear the burden.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [incredulously, raising his head and voice with comic abruptness]
sp.p: Do you mean me, Candida?

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Let us sit and talk comfortably over it like three friends.
Sit down, dear.
sp.stage: [Morell, quite lost, takes the chair from the fireside: the children's chair].
sp.p: Bring me that chair, Eugene.
sp.stage: [She indicates the easy chair. He fetches it silently, even with something like cold strength, and places it next Morell, a little behind him. She sits down. He takes the visitor's chair himself, and sits, inscrutable. When they are all settled she begins, throwing a spell of quietness on them by her calm, sane, tender tone].
sp.p: You remember what you told me about yourself, Eugene: how nobody has cared for you since your old nurse died: how those clever fashionable sisters and successful brothers of yours were your mother's and father's pets: how miserable you were at Eton: how your father is trying to starve you into returning to Oxford: how you have had to live without comfort or welcome or refuge: always lonely, and nearly always disliked and misunderstood, poor boy!

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [faithful to the nobility of his lot]
sp.p: I had my books. I had Nature. And at last I met you.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Never mind that just at present. Now I want you to look at this other boy here: my boy! spoiled from his cradle. We go once a fortnight to see his parents. You should come with us, Eugene, to see the pictures of the hero of that household. James as a baby! the most wonderful of all babies. James holding his first school prize, won at the ripe age of eight! James as the captain of his eleven! James in his first frock coat! James under all sorts of glorious circumstances! You know how strong he is (I hope he didnt hurt you): how clever he is: how happy.

Ask James's mother and his three sisters what it cost to save James the trouble of doing anything but be strong and clever and happy. Ask me what it costs to be James's mother and three sisters and wife and mother to his children all in one. Ask Prossy and Maria how troublesome the house is even when we have no visitors to help us to slice the onions. Ask the tradesmen who want to worry James and spoil his beautiful sermons who it is that puts them off. When there is money to give, he gives it: when there is money to refuse, I refuse it. I build a castle of comfort and indulgence and love for him, and stand sentinel always to keep little vulgar cares out. I make him master here, though he does not know it, and could not tell you a moment ago how it came to be so.
And when he thought I might go away with you, his only anxiety was—what should become of me! And to tempt me to stay he offered me
sp.stage: [leaning forward to stroke his hair caressingly at each phrase]
sp.p: his strength for my defence! his industry for my livelihood! his dignity for my position! his—
ah, I am mixing up your beautiful cadences and spoiling them, am I not, darling?
sp.stage: [She lays her cheek fondly against his].

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.stage: [quite overcome, kneeling beside her chair and embracing her with boyish ingenuousness]
sp.p: It's all true, every word. What I am you have made me with the labor of your hands and the love of your heart. You are my wife, my mother, my sisters: you are the sum of all loving care to me.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Am I your mother and sisters to you, Eugene?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [rising with a fierce gesture of disgust]
sp.p: Ah, never. Out, then, into the night with me!

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: You are not going like that, Eugene?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.stage: [with the ring of a man's voice—no longer a boy's—in the words]
sp.p: I know the hour when it strikes. I am impatient to do what must be done.

sp.speaker: MORELL
sp.p: Candida: dont let him do anything rash.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA
sp.p: Oh, there is no fear. He has learnt to live without happiness.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: I no longer desire happiness: life is nobler than that. Parson James: I give you my happiness with both hands: I love you because you have filled the heart of the woman I loved. Goodbye.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: One last word.
sp.stage: [He stops, but without turning to her. She goes to him].
sp.p: How old are you, Eugene?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS.
sp.p: As old as the world now. This morning I was eighteen.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Eighteen! Will you, for my sake, make a little poem out of the two sentences I am going to say to you? And will you promise to repeat it to yourself whenever you think of me?

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: Say the sentences.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: When I am thirty, she will be forty-five. When I am sixty, she will be seventy-five.

sp.speaker: MARCHBANKS
sp.p: In a hundred years, we shall be the same age. But I have a better secret than that in my heart. Let me go now. The night outside grows impatient.

sp.speaker: CANDIDA.
sp.p: Goodbye.
sp.stage: [She takes his face in her hands; and as he divines her intention and falls on his knees, she kisses his forehead. Then he flies out into the night. She turns to Morell, holding out her arms to him.]
sp.p: Ah, James!

div.stage: They embrace. But they do not know the secret in the poet's heart.
